question: Which period is known to be the trickiest for medication errors and missed care?

options.A: Attending a family gathering on the weekend
options.B: Moving between hospitals, rehab facilities, and home
options.C: Routine visits to the local outdoor market
options.D: Switching from daytime clothes to nightwear

explanation: Correct! Whenever a patient moves from one place of care to another, things easily get mixed up or forgotten. That's why we stay extra alert!

question: Why is it dangerous to give rescue breaths too fast or with too much force?

options.A: It can force air into the stomach and lead to vomiting
options.B: It immediately collapses both lungs due to high pressure
options.C: It causes the patient's heart rate to drop dangerously low
options.D: It forces blood backward into the jugular veins

explanation: Easy does it with breaths! Blowing too hard opens up the stomach instead of the lungs, which can cause the patient to vomit and complicate things.

question: Which test uses actual resistant bacterial spores to confirm your sterilizer worked?

options.A: Visual inspection for dryness
options.B: External chemical tape
options.C: Biological indicators
options.D: Mechanical machine gauges

explanation: Biological indicators contain real, tough spores. If they don't survive the cycle, you know your sterilization process was a total success!

question: How do waterborne diseases like cholera and typhoid usually spread?

options.A: Inhalation of mist from clean cooling towers
options.B: Direct skin contact with industrial chemical waste
options.C: Mosquito bites near stagnant ponds and rivers
options.D: Ingestion of water contaminated with fecal matter

explanation: Correct! These nasty bugs spread mainly when people swallow food or water that has come into contact with human or animal waste.

question: Why must nurses wear gloves or use a tool when applying certain topical medications?

options.A: To keep the patient's room completely sterile
options.B: To prevent absorbing the medication through their own skin
options.C: To prevent the patient from feeling cold during touch
options.D: To ensure the medication absorbs faster into the patient

explanation: Powerful drugs like hormone creams can soak right through your bare hands if you aren't wearing gloves. Always protect yourself too!

question: In which year was the historic Alma-Ata Declaration on Primary Health Care held?
explanation: The landmark international conference that shaped modern community nursing took place in Alma-Ata in 1978. Great to keep in mind for your exams!

question: What is the absolute heart of therapeutic communication in nursing?

options.A: Talking more than the patient talks
options.B: Giving immediate personal advice
options.C: Changing the subject when it gets sad
options.D: Active listening without judgment

explanation: Patients open up when they feel heard and safe. Listening without judging them builds instant trust.

question: Which type of budget is used to purchase expensive, long-term equipment like a new MRI machine?

options.A: Capital budget
options.B: Cash flow budget
options.C: Operating budget
options.D: Personnel budget

explanation: Capital budgets are specifically set aside for large, long-term investments and major equipment. [learn more](GST322_U2_T4#GST322_U2_T4_h3)

question: Which of the following is a major risk factor for puerperal sepsis?

options.A: Rapid spontaneous vaginal birth
options.B: Early ambulation after delivery
options.C: Exclusive breastfeeding
options.D: Prolonged rupture of membranes

explanation: When membranes rupture for a long time before delivery, bacteria have a direct open pathway to travel up into the uterus. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T024#GNS226_U3_T024_h3)

question: When moving a heavy medication cart down a hospital hallway, what is the safest technique?

options.A: Pull the cart behind you for better steering
options.B: Hold the cart with only one hand at all times
options.C: Push the cart rather than pulling it
options.D: Run quickly to minimize the duration of the push

explanation: You got it! Pushing lets you use your body weight and strong leg muscles instead of straining your back and shoulders. [learn more](GNS113_U3_T3#GNS113_U3_T3_h5)

question: Why is routine health monitoring, such as checking blood glucose and blood pressure, essential in day care?

options.A: To detect early signs of chronic disease instability and prevent complications
options.B: To fulfill a legal requirement without any practical clinical value
options.C: To punish clients who fail to follow their prescribed home diets
options.D: To diagnose acute surgical emergencies requiring immediate theater use

explanation: Regular monitoring catches small physiological shifts before they develop into dangerous health crises requiring hospitalization. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T7#GNS324_U5_T7_h6)

question: Which room setup is most important when getting ready for a physical exam?

options.A: Bright flashing lights for visibility
options.B: A cold room temperature to prevent sweating
options.C: Adequate privacy and good lighting
options.D: Open doors to encourage fresh airflow

explanation: Good lighting helps you see subtle skin changes clearly, and privacy helps your patient relax and feel secure with you. Always set the stage for comfort!

question: What is needed to make community health schemes truly successful in Nigeria?

options.A: Government backing, transparent management, and public education
options.B: Making health insurance compulsory only for the wealthy
options.C: Complete elimination of primary health care centers
options.D: Relying solely on foreign donor grants forever

explanation: For long-term success, we need strong support from institutions, honest handling of funds, and well-informed citizens who understand the benefits.

question: What do we call the complete group of people that a researcher is interested in studying?

options.A: Pilot cohort
options.B: Target population
options.C: Control group
options.D: Sample subset

explanation: The target population is the big group that shares the exact traits you want to investigate—like all nursing students in Nigeria, for instance!

question: What is the main feature of a community-based organization (CBO)?

options.A: It is formed and run by members of the local community
options.B: It is managed by international foreign diplomats
options.C: It operates exclusively in capital city headquarters
options.D: It focuses only on manufacturing pharmaceutical drugs

explanation: You got it! CBOs start from within the grassroots, meaning they truly understand local needs and how to solve them.

question: What is another common name for Gallows traction?

options.A: Balanced suspension
options.B: Russell's traction
options.C: Bryant's traction
options.D: Buck's extension

explanation: You'll often hear Gallows traction called Bryant's traction in the ward! It's named after the surgeon who first used it to help young children heal. You've got this!

question: How do cancer cells frequently manipulate apoptosis to survive and multiply?

options.A: They trigger excessive external death receptor signals
options.B: They replace damaged mitochondria with healthy ones
options.C: They mutate regulatory genes to evade programmed cell death
options.D: They speed up the intrinsic pathway to destroy healthy tissue

explanation: Cancer cells often survive by disabling the normal suicide signals that would normally force a damaged cell to die. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h7)

question: Why is community profiling necessary before launching a health project?

options.A: It prevents outsiders from visiting the community
options.B: It automatically cures local malnutrition cases
options.C: It proves to the government that nurses are working hard
options.D: It reveals the unique demographics and culture of the area

explanation: Profiling gives health workers clear baseline data about who lives there and how they live, guiding appropriate planning. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T5#GNS124_U4_T5_h2)

question: What is the primary hormonal cause of insulin resistance during the second and third trimesters of pregnancy?

options.A: Human placental lactogen
options.B: Oxytocin
options.C: Follicle stimulating hormone
options.D: Thyroid stimulating hormone

explanation: Placental hormones like human placental lactogen actively block maternal insulin to keep enough glucose in the blood for the growing baby. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T006#GNS226_U4_T006_h1)

question: You are preparing a suction catheter for an adult patient with an artificial airway. What is the rule of thumb for selecting the catheter size?

options.A: It must be the largest possible size that fits through the opening
options.B: It should always be a uniform size 14 French regardless of the tube
options.C: It should fill the entire inside of the tube to grab all the mucus
options.D: It should take up no more than half the inner diameter of the airway

explanation: Leaving enough open space around the catheter prevents a vacuum from forming inside the lungs, which would dangerously drop oxygen levels. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T12#GNS212_U2_T12_h3)

question: In human nutrition, what exactly is a kilocalorie (kcal)?

options.A: The speed at which glucose enters the bloodstream
options.B: The heat needed to raise one kilogram of water by one degree Celsius
options.C: The amount of sodium dissolved in a liquid
options.D: The total protein weight inside a food item

explanation: A kilocalorie is just a unit of heat energy. It tells us the amount of energy needed to raise the temperature of a kilo of water by 1°C. Simple physics applied to food!

question: A kitchen worker comes in with a sudden case of watery diarrhea and a mild fever. What should be done immediately?

options.A: Ask them to wash dishes with hot water instead
options.B: Take them off food handling duties right away
options.C: Tell them to swallow an anti-diarrhea drug and keep working
options.D: Let them work as long as they wear two pairs of gloves

explanation: Any worker showing signs of a tummy bug must be kept away from food immediately to stop germs from spreading to everyone else.

question: Which nutritional deficiency significantly increases a patient's risk of getting pressure sores?

options.A: Protein deficiency
options.B: Sodium overload
options.C: Vitamin C excess
options.D: Carbohydrate restriction

explanation: Protein is like the building blocks for healthy skin. Without enough protein, the skin becomes weak, fragile, and takes forever to repair itself! [learn more](GNS112_U5_T6#GNS112_U5_T6_h3)

question: A nurse notices that two different injectable drugs have very similar label designs and are stored right next to each other. What is the best immediate risk reduction action?

options.A: Report the labeling issue to pharmacy and management and separate the drugs
options.B: Wait until a medication error actually happens before telling anyone
options.C: Tell the patients not to accept any injections from other staff
options.D: Hide one of the drugs in a private pocket so nobody else uses it

explanation: Spotted look-alike hazards should be immediately separated and reported to prevent a future mix-up. [learn more](GST319_U4_T6#GST319_U4_T6_h6)

question: During which stage of an infection do mild, general symptoms like tiredness first show up before full sickness hits?

options.A: Incubation period
options.B: Prodromal stage
options.C: Convalescent stage
options.D: Illness stage

explanation: Well done! The prodromal stage is that early phase where a patient just feels 'off' or unusually tired before specific symptoms appear.

question: A nurse is teaching a patient how to do Kegel exercises correctly. What is the key instruction?

options.A: Contract the pelvic floor muscles as if trying to stop the flow of urine
options.B: Squeeze the abdominal and thigh muscles tightly while holding your breath
options.C: Push down gently as if having a bowel movement
options.D: Flex the buttocks and hips until your pelvis rises off the bed

explanation: Spot on! Kegels are all about squeezing those pelvic floor muscles—just like you're pausing your urine stream mid-flow, without squeezing your tummy or thighs.

question: What is a key feature of how Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF / Doctors Without Borders) operates?

options.A: Focusing solely on long-term structural economic development
options.B: Strict independence from government political agendas
options.C: Operating strictly as a financing body for local hospitals
options.D: Requiring formal government approval before assessing any crisis

explanation: Brilliant! Because MSF relies on private donations, they can stay completely independent and care for people purely based on need, no politics attached.

question: How often should you reposition an immobile neurological patient to protect their skin?

options.A: Only when requested
options.B: Every two hours
options.C: Once every shift
options.D: Every six hours

explanation: Turning patients every two hours takes the pressure off bony areas, which is one of the best ways to stop pressure sores from forming.

question: A patient asks why her body doesn't reject the developing pregnancy as a foreign object. What is the best way to explain this?

options.A: The baby carries the exact same blood type as the mother always
options.B: The placenta completely blocks all maternal blood cells from forming
options.C: The mother's immune system shuts down completely during pregnancy
options.D: The outer trophoblast layer actively modifies local immune responses

explanation: The placenta and outer cells are clever—they whisper to the immune system to stay calm so the baby can grow safely. Clinical communication made simple!

question: Which of these is NOT a good way to prevent medication errors?

options.A: Minimizing hallway conversations while calculating doses
options.B: Double-checking high-alert calculations with a colleague
options.C: Carefully reading medication labels three separate times
options.D: Rushing through drug rounds to finish ahead of schedule

explanation: Spot on! Rushing causes stress and mistakes. Taking your time is key to safe medication administration.

question: Why is the variable region of an antibody so important?

options.A: It allows the body to recognize many different antigens
options.B: It provides the structural strength to hold the Y shape
options.C: It helps the antibody attach to normal red blood cells
options.D: It dissolves the cell wall of invading bacteria directly

explanation: Because our bodies face countless different germs, the variable region acts like a shape-shifter at the tips of the antibody, creating diverse binding sites to lock onto various invaders.

question: Which of these is a common health problem that shows up after a major disaster?

options.A: Psychological trauma and PTSD
options.B: Increased availability of specialized surgeons
options.C: Immediate financial surplus
options.D: Enhanced community infrastructure

explanation: Great job! Survivors often deal with deep emotional distress and mental health challenges long after their physical wounds heal.

question: How is Type II FGM different from Type I?

options.A: It only affects internal reproductive organs like the uterus.
options.B: It involves more extensive tissue removal including the labia minora.
options.C: It is performed exclusively in hospital operating theatres.
options.D: It does not involve any form of scarring or healing complications.

explanation: Spot on! Type II builds on Type I by also removing the labia minora.

question: A nurse wants to test a 15-year-old patient for Chlamydia. Which diagnostic test is the most sensitive and reliable?

options.A: Nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs)
options.B: Visual inspection of mucosal tissues
options.C: Urine dipstick analysis for protein
options.D: Routine microscopic blood cell counts

explanation: Correct! NAATs are the gold standard for spotting bacterial STIs like chlamydia using a simple urine sample or swab.

question: When is an individual digital message most appropriate in a clinical setting?

options.A: For posting general holiday notices on a public forum
options.B: For broadcasting emergency drills to the whole hospital
options.C: For publishing weekly hospital menus to the general public
options.D: For sharing quick, specific updates about a single patient

explanation: One-on-one digital messages are ideal for targeted, rapid communication regarding a specific patient's immediate needs. [learn more](GNS113_U3_T5#GNS113_U3_T5_h2)

question: What is a major non-medical challenge that delays emergency survival in many developing areas?

options.A: Strict government regulations on the use of intravenous fluids
options.B: A lack of interest in modern medicine among rural community members
options.C: Delays in reaching a health facility due to financial and transport challenges
options.D: Excessive availability of free ambulance services on major roads

explanation: Transportation bottlenecks and money hurdles often delay patients from getting to the hospital on time. Every minute counts in an emergency!

question: What happens to the spread of disease if a nurse successfully breaks even one link in the chain of infection?

options.A: The pathogen automatically changes into a harmless bacteria
options.B: The patient develops instant immunity against all other germs
options.C: The infection cycle is stopped and disease spread is prevented
options.D: The reservoir completely disappears from the environment

explanation: Because the chain requires every single link to function, breaking just one link halts the entire transmission process. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T6#GNS313_U1_T6_h2)

question: What kind of services are typically provided at the secondary health care level?

options.A: Traditional herbal medicine manufacturing
options.B: General hospital care and emergency surgeries
options.C: Routine childhood immunization in village squares
options.D: Advanced medical research and space medicine

explanation: Secondary facilities like general hospitals handle referrals from primary clinics and provide more specialized inpatient and surgical care. [learn more](GST322_U5_T2#GST322_U5_T2_h2)

question: How do you check for pain in a critical care patient who is intubated and unable to speak?

options.A: By asking family members how much pain is present
options.B: By assuming intubated patients cannot feel pain
options.C: By waiting until the patient's blood pressure drops
options.D: By observing facial expressions and muscle tension

explanation: When words aren't an option, watch their body! Frowning, tense muscles, and restlessness tell a clear story.

question: When is an autocratic leadership style most appropriate in a clinical setting?

options.A: When planning monthly work rosters
options.B: During routine staff meetings
options.C: When mentoring a new nursing student
options.D: During a sudden cardiac arrest

explanation: High-pressure emergencies require quick, centralized command and clear orders, making autocratic leadership necessary. [learn more](GST321_U3_T3#GST321_U3_T3_h2)

question: A patient takes double their prescribed pain medication to get fast relief for a toothache. What is this called?

options.A: Casual substance use
options.B: Substance misuse
options.C: Normal recovery process
options.D: True physical addiction

explanation: Misuse simply means using a medication in a way other than how it was prescribed—like taking an extra dose on your own. Keep up the good work!

question: What was a major focus of nursing research during the 1970s and 1980s?

options.A: Eliminating the need for clinical bedside nurses
options.B: Studying hospital kitchen sanitation procedures
options.C: Designing hospital computer software systems
options.D: Developing distinct nursing theories and models

explanation: Nurses during this era worked hard to create their own theoretical frameworks rather than relying solely on medical or psychological models. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T3#GNS217_U2_T3_h4)

question: Why does cholera spread so fast during heavy rains and floods in crowded areas?

options.A: Mosquito populations multiply rapidly in stagnant pools of water.
options.B: Floodwaters easily contaminate public drinking water sources with sewage.
options.C: Airborne dust carries the cholera bacteria across long distances.
options.D: Cold weather lowers human immune systems against bacterial toxins.

explanation: Cholera is waterborne! When floodwaters mix with sewage, people accidentally drink contaminated water, leading to rapid outbreaks.

question: Reviewing existing clinic registers and local government health reports is an example of which data collection method?

options.A: Experimental data collection
options.B: Secondary data collection
options.C: Primary data collection
options.D: Biological data collection

explanation: Using already recorded data from registers and reports is classed as secondary data because it was collected by someone else previously. [learn more](GNS225_U2_T15#GNS225_U2_T15_h2)

question: What does having an 'appreciation for a system' mean in a busy hospital setting?

options.A: Ensuring every single department makes a profit
options.B: Keeping hospital departments strictly separated so no one gets distracted
options.C: Recognizing how different departments depend on each other to reach a common goal
options.D: Giving regular awards to hardworking nursing staff

explanation: Think of a hospital like a football team—pharmacy, lab, and nursing all have to pass the ball to each other to win for the patient!

question: Why should hospitals offer counseling and support to nurses involved in errors?

options.A: To help them process their trauma and prevent severe burnout
options.B: To prevent them from talking to hospital management ever again
options.C: To ensure they can be easily monitored for future illegal activities
options.D: To replace their clinical training with psychological theory

explanation: Clinical errors take a heavy emotional toll. Providing support helps nurses heal and protects them from burning out.

question: Which counselling approach features the clinician taking a strong, expert role to give direct instructions?

options.A: Non-directive counselling
options.B: Peer support counselling
options.C: Community outreach counselling
options.D: Directive counselling

explanation: In directive counselling, the clinician provides clear, firm guidance and instructions on what the patient must do. [learn more](GNS227_U7_T002#GNS227_U7_T002_h6)

question: Which of the following is a frequent long-term complication of poorly treated acute osteomyelitis?

options.A: Rheumatoid arthritis
options.B: Iron deficiency anemia
options.C: Type 1 diabetes mellitus
options.D: Chronic osteomyelitis

explanation: When acute bone infections are not fully eradicated, they frequently transition into long-standing chronic osteomyelitis with recurrent flare-ups. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T17#GNS222_U1_T17_h10)

question: What usually happens on the ward when a nurse struggles with poor time management?

options.A: Decreased physical fatigue among nursing staff
options.B: Higher patient satisfaction scores across the unit
options.C: Increased risk of missed care and medication errors
options.D: More time available for professional development

explanation: True! When things get too rushed and we lose control of our time, important tasks or meds can easily slip through the cracks. Take a breath—learning how to pace yourself helps prevent this!

question: What is the medical term for the natural weakening of the immune system that happens as people get older?

options.A: Immunosenescence
options.B: Hypersensitivity
options.C: Autoimmunity
options.D: Seroconversion

explanation: Well done! 'Immuno' relates to the immune system, and 'senescence' means growing older. Put them together and you get the age-related decline in immunity.

question: Why are role-playing and peer education so effective in school health classes?

options.A: Students prefer playing games over reading textbooks
options.B: Interactive methods remove the need for qualified teachers
options.C: Government policies ban traditional classroom lecturing
options.D: Health habits are behavioral and require active practice

explanation: Spot on! Health education is all about changing daily actions, which works best when students actually practice what they are learning.

question: When a researcher collects 'primary data', what are they doing?

options.A: Records taken from old hospital admission logs from ten years ago
options.B: Data published in international textbooks without any author names
options.C: Information collected directly by the researcher for the current study
options.D: Information guessed by the nurse without asking the patient

explanation: That's correct! Primary data is freshly gathered firsthand by the investigator specifically for their current study.

question: What does a high amount of out-of-pocket health spending usually tell us about a country?

options.A: A weak public financial safety net for citizens
options.B: An exceptionally strong and free healthcare system
options.C: That citizens pay very low taxes overall
options.D: That the government is meeting all international health targets

explanation: When patients have to pay cash for almost everything at the hospital, it usually means the government's safety net isn't quite covering them yet.

question: An IV infusion of 1000 mL normal saline is ordered to run over 8 hours using an electronic pump. What is the rate in mL/hr?

options.A: 125 mL/hr
options.B: 150 mL/hr
options.C: 100 mL/hr
options.D: 80 mL/hr

explanation: Divide the total volume (1000 mL) by the total hours (8 hours) to get 125 mL/hr. [learn more](GNS125_U2_T6#GNS125_U2_T6_h6)

question: What is the main idea behind family-centred care when nursing an infant?

options.A: Allowing the nurse to make all home care choices
options.B: Treating the infant as part of a family unit
options.C: Focusing solely on the medical needs of the baby
options.D: Isolating the infant from other family members

explanation: Spot on! Family-centred care treats the baby and the family as one team, making sure you work closely with the loved ones who know the child best.

question: What should a primary care nurse do AFTER referring a high-risk patient to a general hospital?

options.A: Send a bill to the ministry of health for transport expenses
options.B: Follow up to check if the patient reached the hospital and received care
options.C: Wait ten years before asking the family about the patient's condition
options.D: Assume the patient is completely cured and remove their record from the file

explanation: Our job doesn't end when we hand over the referral letter. Following up ensures the patient actually arrived and is getting the care they need!

question: Which supplement is given to pregnant women to help prevent neural tube defects?

options.A: Vitamin C
options.B: Potassium chloride
options.C: Zinc gluconate
options.D: Folic acid

explanation: Folic acid is a super important vitamin during early pregnancy. It helps the baby's brain and spinal cord develop properly.

question: Which common side effect of opioids do patients almost NEVER develop a tolerance to?

options.A: Nausea
options.B: Constipation
options.C: Euphoria
options.D: Sedation

explanation: While patients get used to the sleepiness and dizziness from opioids, the bowels stay slow. Always plan for laxatives!

question: Which of these is NOT a serious warning sign covered by the ACHES mnemonic?

options.A: Severe pain and swelling in the lower leg
options.B: Mild morning nausea and mild breast tenderness
options.C: Severe chest pain and shortness of breath
options.D: Sudden severe headaches with visual disturbances

explanation: Mild nausea and tender breasts are normal, everyday side effects when starting hormones. ACHES is meant to catch the rare, serious red flags!

question: A patient has a leaky mitral valve. Where will blood wrongly flow when the ventricles squeeze?

options.A: Forward into the pulmonary veins
options.B: Forward into the aorta
options.C: Back into the left atrium
options.D: Back into the right ventricle

explanation: Since the mitral valve sits right between the left upper and lower chambers (atrium and ventricle), a weak seal lets blood slip backward upstairs instead of going forward into the body.

question: What happens during a prescribing cascade?

options.A: The pharmacy runs out of basic supplies and substitutes vitamins
options.B: A drug side effect is mistaken for a new illness and treated with another drug
options.C: All medications are washed out of the patient's system at once
options.D: A nurse stops all prescriptions due to a sudden power outage

explanation: The prescribing cascade creates a dangerous cycle where side effects lead to more prescriptions instead of drug discontinuation. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T7#GNS215_U1_T7_h3)

question: Why does cigarette smoking strongly increase the risk of bladder cancer?

options.A: Tobacco smoke reduces blood flow to the external genitalia
options.B: Carcinogens from tobacco are filtered by the kidneys and sit in the bladder
options.C: Nicotine directly damages the muscular layers of the ureters
options.D: Smoking completely stops the bladder walls from expanding properly

explanation: When someone smokes, the toxic chemicals enter their bloodstream. The kidneys filter these out into the urine, where they sit in the bladder and irritate the lining over time.

question: When is a return-to-work medical examination performed?

options.A: Before a new worker signs their initial employment contract
options.B: Every month as a routine check for all factory staff members
options.C: After an employee recovers from an illness or injury and prepares to resume duties
options.D: Immediately after a major chemical spill occurs on site

explanation: Spot on! This check ensures the worker is fully ready to return or tells us if they need lighter duties to avoid getting hurt again.

question: What is one major perk of condoms over hormonal birth control pills?

options.A: Condoms require no action at the time of intercourse
options.B: Condoms cause permanent changes in fertility
options.C: Condoms have a much higher real-world perfection rate
options.D: Condoms offer protection against sexually transmitted infections

explanation: You got it! While pills are great for preventing pregnancy, only barrier methods like condoms protect against STIs too.

question: What is the main goal of contact tracing during an epidemic?

options.A: To punish individuals who broke quarantine rules
options.B: To distribute free food items to sick patients
options.C: To collect financial donations for the clinic
options.D: To find and monitor people exposed to an infected person

explanation: Correct! Contact tracing helps us spot exposed individuals early so we can monitor or treat them before they spread the infection further.

question: How does Psychological First Aid differ from traditional psychotherapy?

options.A: PFA involves prescribing psychiatric medications
options.B: PFA requires a licensed psychiatrist to perform it
options.C: PFA focuses on practical needs rather than analyzing trauma
options.D: PFA is only used weeks after the disaster has ended

explanation: PFA avoids asking survivors to relive or analyze their traumatic experience, focusing instead on comfort and basic needs. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T6#GNS315_U5_T6_h6)

question: Why is having a strong network connection so crucial for electronic health records?

options.A: It allows real-time updating and sharing of patient data across different departments.
options.B: It prevents computer hardware from overheating during heavy computational tasks.
options.C: It converts analog audio alarms into clear digital text messages.
options.D: It automatically increases the storage capacity of the local hard drive.

explanation: Real-time networking means the pharmacy, lab, and your ward see the exact same up-to-the-minute patient info instantly!

question: What is the main goal of patient safety in healthcare?

options.A: To eliminate the cost of hospital stays
options.B: To ensure doctors make all clinical choices
options.C: To speed up the hospital discharge process
options.D: To prevent accidental harm to patients

explanation: Patient safety is all about keeping patients protected from accidental injury or harm while they are receiving care from us. You've got this!

question: Which of the following is NOT an effective strategy for preventing the spread of gastroenteritis in a community?

options.A: Giving rotavirus vaccines to young infants
options.B: Using over-the-counter antidiarrheal drugs daily
options.C: Washing hands regularly with soap and clean water
options.D: Ensuring access to safe and treated drinking water

explanation: Daily antidiarrheal drugs do not prevent infections or transmission; hygiene, safe water, and vaccination are the true preventive measures. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T20#GNS313_U2_T20_h6)

question: What does the Latin name 'dura mater' mean in plain English?

options.A: Soft tender
options.B: Thin web
options.C: Web-like mother
options.D: Tough mother

explanation: Spot on! 'Dura' means tough or hard, so it translates to tough mother—a fitting name for this thick, leathery protector.

question: A patient has swollen ankles, bulging neck veins, and crackles in the lungs. What do these signs point to?

options.A: Fluid overload
options.B: Vitamin deficiency
options.C: Acute protein loss
options.D: Severe dehydration

explanation: When water builds up in the tissues and lungs, you get swelling, bulging veins, and lung crackles. That's fluid overload!

question: Which tool do event managers commonly use to watch crowd movement and density in real time?

options.A: Post-event questionnaires
options.B: Weekly weather forecasts
options.C: Closed-circuit television cameras
options.D: Paper registration logs

explanation: CCTV camera feeds give security and medical teams 'eyes everywhere' so they can spot crowd build-ups instantly.

question: What is the biggest superpower of using radio broadcasts for health messages in rural areas?

options.A: They allow the nurse to physically examine patients through the radio wave.
options.B: They are completely free to produce and require no electricity or batteries.
options.C: They can reach massive, dispersed populations simultaneously across vast distances.
options.D: They replace the need for face-to-face community health nursing entirely.

explanation: Radio cuts across bad roads and long distances, letting you share vital health tips with thousands of people at the exact same time!

question: Finding Escherichia coli (E. coli) in a water sample tells you what?

options.A: High concentrations of industrial heavy metals
options.B: Recent fecal contamination from humans or animals
options.C: Excessive mineral hardness from underground rocks
options.D: A normal and safe level of plant nutrients

explanation: Spot on! E. coli is our warning flag. Its presence proves that waste matter has found its way into the water supply.

question: Which hormone is the main one responsible for lowering your blood sugar after you eat a meal?

options.A: Cortisol
options.B: Glucagon
options.C: Insulin
options.D: Adrenaline

explanation: Spot on! Insulin is released by your pancreas to help glucose move out of your bloodstream and into your body cells to give you energy.

question: What does intersectoral collaboration mean in community health practice?

options.A: Transferring all sick patients directly to tertiary teaching hospitals without delay
options.B: Working together with non-health sectors like agriculture and education to improve health
options.C: Merging all community health clinics under one central government ministry
options.D: Requiring nurses to perform the duties of doctors and pharmacists simultaneously

explanation: Intersectoral collaboration involves partnering with different sectors outside health because social determinants of health span multiple fields. [learn more](GNS225_U2_T26#GNS225_U2_T26_h7)

question: What is the main purpose of emergency classification in nursing?

options.A: Determining which nurse works which shift
options.B: Sorting patients based on medical urgency
options.C: Reducing the total number of hospital admissions
options.D: Calculating the final hospital bill for the patient

explanation: Emergency classification helps nurses quickly organize patients by how sick they are so the most critical ones get treated first. [learn more](GNS315_U2_T1#GNS315_U2_T1_h1)

question: Why does a nurse need an N95 respirator instead of a standard surgical mask when caring for a patient with tuberculosis?

options.A: Airborne diseases can only be stopped if the nurse wears double face shields
options.B: Surgical masks are only designed to protect patients from the nurse's own breath
options.C: Tuberculosis is airborne, meaning tiny infectious particles float in the air and require tight filtration
options.D: Tuberculosis bacteria can easily dissolve through the thin material of a regular surgical mask

explanation: Standard surgical masks let tiny airborne particles slip through the sides, whereas N95 respirators seal tightly to filter out microscopic droplet nuclei. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T6#GNS313_U1_T6_h5)

question: What is a key benefit of offering structured social activities in assisted living?

options.A: Replacing the need for family visits altogether
options.B: Reducing the cost of building maintenance
options.C: Combating feelings of loneliness and depression
options.D: Eliminating the need for any routine medical care

explanation: Group activities and social events help keep residents engaged, active, and emotionally connected, reducing isolation and depression. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T6#GNS324_U5_T6_h6)

question: Why is strict hand hygiene and infection control extra important when caring for an immunodeficient patient?

options.A: To prevent the nurse from catching germs from the hospital floor
options.B: To protect the patient from opportunistic pathogens they cannot fight off
options.C: To keep the patient's room smelling clean and fresh
options.D: To stop the patient's medication from causing skin rashes

explanation: Spot on! Germs that wouldn't bother a healthy person can easily overwhelm someone whose immune system is down.

question: During a home visit, a nurse sees a parole patient acting paranoid, talking to unseen things, and throwing away meds. What is the nurse's priority?

options.A: Tell the patient's neighbors to handle the situation.
options.B: Report it to the care team right away to prevent a full relapse.
options.C: Wait three weeks until the next scheduled doctor visit.
options.D: Ignore it since the patient is living outside the hospital now.

explanation: Spot on! Paranoid behavior and tossing medications are urgent red flags. Acting fast helps the team step in before things escalate.

question: Along with testing the AED machine itself, what other crucial item must you check regularly?

options.A: Test the manual defibrillator paddle synchronization cables
options.B: Measure the electrical resistance of the backup wall charger
options.C: Verify the expiration dates of the adhesive electrode pads
options.D: Inspect the mechanical springs inside the chest compression board

explanation: Always check those pad expiration dates! The conductive gel on the pads dries out over time, making them useless if they expire.

question: Staff nurses complain of severe exhaustion. Instead of just adding extra shifts, the manager investigates and discovers that broken equipment is causing major delays. What has the manager found?

options.A: A completely unrelated administrative task
options.B: The root cause of the exhaustion
options.C: An entirely programmed routine choice
options.D: The personal fault of the junior nurses

explanation: Brilliant! By looking past the surface complaints, the manager found the true source of the trouble.

question: A village has no local markets, poor farming land, and high unemployment. What health issue is most likely to spike here?

options.A: Stress-related injuries from high-speed driving
options.B: Malnutrition and poverty-related illnesses
options.C: Occupational hazards from heavy factory work
options.D: Complications from cosmetic plastic surgeries

explanation: Exactly. When the local economy struggles and people can't get basic food or income, malnutrition and poverty-related health issues naturally follow.

question: You see a toddler running around the living room while eating crackers. What should you do first?

options.A: Wait until the child finishes running to intervene.
options.B: Take the food away immediately and scold the child.
options.C: Calmly ask the child to sit at the table before eating more.
options.D: Offer the child a cup of water to wash down the crackers.

explanation: Great nursing judgment! Running and eating is a major recipe for choking. Gently guiding them to sit down keeps them safe with a smile.

question: Which group benefits the most from attending a sheltered workshop?

options.A: Skilled healthcare professionals returning from sabbatical
options.B: Healthy young adults seeking high-paying corporate careers
options.C: Experienced artisans looking for advanced technical training
options.D: Individuals with chronic psychiatric or intellectual disabilities

explanation: These workshops are specially tailored for people whose health challenges make it difficult to jump straight into standard jobs. Keep up the good work!

question: Which event is classified as an immunization error-related adverse event?

options.A: A child developing a mild fever due to an immune response
options.B: A mild allergic rash caused by an egg protein allergy
options.C: An abscess forming due to unsterile injection techniques
options.D: A baby catching an unrelated malaria infection the next day

explanation: Immunization errors happen due to mistakes in handling, preparation, or administration, such as introducing bacteria through poor aseptic technique. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T61#GNS214_U1_T61_h7)

question: How should a nurse respond when a community attributes an illness to traditional or spiritual causes?

options.A: Report the village elders to the police for spreading misinformation
options.B: Mock their beliefs openly during the public health outreach meeting
options.C: Refuse to distribute any IEC materials until they change their religion
options.D: Acknowledge their perspective respectfully while gently introducing health education

explanation: Respect is key! By honoring their views first, you open the door to share health education without causing offense.

question: What does informed consent guarantee a research participant?

options.A: They will receive free lifetime medical care from the teaching hospital
options.B: Their names will be published on the front page of local newspapers
options.C: They are legally required to complete every single interview question
options.D: They understand the study and can withdraw at any time without penalty

explanation: Participation is totally voluntary! Patients must know what they are getting into and can walk away whenever they want.

question: Why is spreading unverified rumors during an emergency response so dangerous?

options.A: It increases the battery life of digital tracking dashboards
options.B: It automatically improves the physical infrastructure of the command center
options.C: It speeds up the distribution of medical supplies to remote areas
options.D: It can cause public panic and lead to the misallocation of ambulances and resources

explanation: False rumors cause chaos, often sending critical ambulances and rescue teams to places that don't actually need them.

question: What is the name of the suture that separates the two parietal bones along the top of the fetal head?

options.A: Sagittal suture
options.B: Coronal suture
options.C: Frontal suture
options.D: Lambdoidal suture

explanation: The sagittal suture runs right along the midline at the top of the head, dividing the left and right parietal bones. [learn more](GNS121_U6_T14#GNS121_U6_T14_h1)

question: If you hear fine crackling sounds in a patient's lower lung fields using your stethoscope, what does that usually mean?

options.A: Complete obstruction of the trachea
options.B: Fluid accumulation in the alveoli
options.C: Enlargement of the primary bronchi
options.D: Severe spasm of the vocal cords

explanation: Brilliant! Those crackles happen when tiny, fluid-filled or sticky air sacs pop open as the patient breathes in.

question: How does home care primarily change the way healthcare is delivered?

options.A: From hospital-centered interventions to daily life
options.B: From professional nursing to family-only treatment
options.C: From chronic disease management to acute surgery
options.D: From everyday living to rigid facility schedules

explanation: Instead of keeping care locked inside hospital walls, home nursing brings support directly into the patient's personal living space.

question: What is the big giveaway that a study is observational?

options.A: Patients are given a new medication to test its safety
options.B: The researcher does not apply any experimental intervention
options.C: Data is collected exclusively through laboratory blood tests
options.D: All participants must be followed up for at least ten years

explanation: Exactly! In observational studies, researchers just sit back, watch, and record what happens naturally without interfering. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T13#GNS217_U3_T13_h3)

question: How do grief and mourning differ from each other?

options.A: Grief is a medical diagnosis, while mourning is a nursing intervention
options.B: Grief only happens in hospitals, while mourning happens at home
options.C: Grief is the internal emotional feeling, while mourning is the outward expression
options.D: Grief lasts for years, while mourning ends after a few days

explanation: Think of grief as what happens inside your heart and mind, while mourning is how you show it on the outside through cultural or religious practices.

question: Why is it important to clearly define the scope of a community health assessment?

options.A: It shortens the nursing shift schedule for the week
options.B: It eliminates the need to talk to community members
options.C: It guarantees that zero diseases will occur in the area
options.D: It keeps the assessment focused on specific health problems

explanation: Communities have many needs, but trying to fix everything at once can overwhelm your team. Setting a clear scope helps you stay focused and realistic!

question: Ten minutes after delivery, a mum starts bleeding heavily and her uterus feels soft and boggy. What should you do right away?

options.A: Encourage the mother to walk around the room to boost circulation
options.B: Wait patiently for thirty minutes to see if the bleeding stops on its own
options.C: Send the patient home immediately with iron tablets
options.D: Perform fundal massage and administer the prescribed uterotonic drug

explanation: Well done! Massaging the uterus helps it contract, and giving the uterotonic medication stops the bleeding fast.

question: What is the main law protecting the rights of children in Nigeria?

options.A: The Adult Criminal Code
options.B: The Child Rights Act
options.C: The Public Land Decree
options.D: The National Health Insurance Act

explanation: Spot on! The Child Rights Act is the key legal framework safeguarding the welfare and special protection of minors in Nigeria.

question: What is the most frequent cause of heavy bleeding after delivery (postpartum hemorrhage) in grand multiparous women?

options.A: Uterine atony
options.B: Uterine inversion
options.C: Retained placental fragments
options.D: Cervical laceration

explanation: Uterine atony happens when the womb muscles fail to clamp down tightly after the baby is born, leaving blood vessels wide open to bleed.

question: What is the main focus of the public health sector?

options.A: Providing elective cosmetic surgery at discounted rates
options.B: Manufacturing pharmaceuticals for international export only
options.C: Population-level health and disease prevention for all citizens
options.D: Generating maximum financial profit for shareholder investors

explanation: Public health is all about protecting the community as a whole, making sure everyone has access to care rather than worrying about profits.

question: What is the job of a cerumenolytic drug like carbamide peroxide?

options.A: To numb the ear canal before minor procedures
options.B: To kill bacteria causing deep ear infections
options.C: To soften and break down hard earwax for easy removal
options.D: To dry up fluid draining from the eardrum

explanation: Cerumenolytics do exactly what their name suggests: they break down stubborn, impacted earwax so it's a breeze to clear out of the canal.

question: Why is it helpful for nurses to understand basic cell biology when giving medications?

options.A: Cells manufacture all oral medications inside the cytoplasm before absorption
options.B: Nurses must count the number of patient cells before calculating dosages
options.C: Medications only work if they completely destroy the plasma membrane
options.D: Drugs often target specific cellular receptors and mechanisms to create their effects

explanation: Spot on! Most drugs work by locking onto specific targets on or inside our cells. Knowing how cells work helps you understand why medicines do what they do in the body.

question: Which common childhood condition should a psychiatric nurse screen for alongside a behaviour disorder?

options.A: Iron deficiency anemia
options.B: Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder
options.C: Type 1 diabetes mellitus
options.D: Chronic kidney disease

explanation: Behaviour disorders frequently happen right alongside conditions like ADHD, depression, or anxiety. Screening for all of them ensures holistic care!

question: What main thing defines 'special groups' in community health?

options.A: Having a very high financial income
options.B: Belonging to a particular political party
options.C: Higher health risks and limited access to care
options.D: Living exclusively in capital cities

explanation: You nailed it! Special groups are populations that face higher health vulnerabilities and struggle more to get standard healthcare. Knowing who they are helps us direct our care where it's needed most.

question: Which major international conference linked population policy directly with human rights?

options.A: The Geneva Convention on the Treatment of Patients
options.B: The Alma-Ata Declaration on Primary Health Care
options.C: The 1994 International Conference on Population and Development in Cairo
options.D: The 1995 World Conference on Women held in Beijing

explanation: It's the 1994 Cairo Conference! This was a massive turning point that shifted global health focus toward empowering individuals and protecting their rights.

question: What does 'capacity building' by an NGO usually look like in a community?

options.A: Auditing government financial accounts annually
options.B: Replacing all doctors with foreign medical specialists
options.C: Constructing large teaching hospitals in major capital cities
options.D: Training local volunteers and birth attendants to educate communities

explanation: Capacity building is all about empowering locals! By teaching community members new skills, health programs can keep running long after the NGO leaves.

question: What is a major barrier that stops eligible people from using public food support systems?

options.A: Bureaucratic hurdles and social stigma associated with asking for help
options.B: The requirement to pass a physical fitness test before enrolling
options.C: Government rules that ban people who have a job from applying
options.D: The excessive high quality of food provided in these programs

explanation: Complicated paperwork and the fear of being judged often discourage people from getting the food support they need. Don't worry, every question helps you grow!

question: Which of the following is NOT a standard precaution practice?

options.A: Using a private negative-pressure room for every patient
options.B: Performing hand hygiene before and after patient contact
options.C: Using safe injection practices and proper sharps disposal
options.D: Wearing gloves when touching non-intact skin or body fluids

explanation: Negative-pressure rooms are special transmission-based precautions for airborne germs, not a routine standard precaution for everyone. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T81#GNS214_U1_T81_h6)

question: Why is community handover so important at the end of a health project?

options.A: To prevent community members from ever asking questions about the budget
options.B: To legally transfer ownership of the clinic building to the nursing staff
options.C: To ensure local structures keep health activities running after project staff leave
options.D: To permanently cut off government funding to the local health district

explanation: Handover guarantees sustainability. We want the community to keep taking charge of their health long after our project team packs up.

question: How do patients dealing with heavy stress often present themselves in the clinic?

options.A: With sudden weight gain and lower blood pressure
options.B: With visible joy and high energy levels
options.C: With physical complaints like headaches, insomnia, and body pains
options.D: With enhanced memory and sharp focus

explanation: Emotional stress loves to hide in physical symptoms. When patients can't sleep or have endless body aches, stress is often the culprit!

question: At what age should complementary foods be introduced to an infant?

options.A: At three months of age
options.B: At six months of age
options.C: At nine months of age
options.D: At one year of age

explanation: Around six months, breast milk alone can't keep up with the baby's growing iron and energy demands. That's when safe complementary foods come in!

question: A student wants to study 'hospital stress'. Which option is a well-focused, realistic research topic?

options.A: Reviewing the history of global healthcare systems
options.B: Comparing the salaries of all hospital workers worldwide
options.C: Assessing night-shift burnout among intensive care unit nurses
options.D: Finding out why people get stressed in all buildings

explanation: Great research topics are narrow and specific! Focusing on a particular group (ICU nurses) and issue (night-shift burnout) makes your study much easier to manage.

question: How does positive pressure ventilation differ from how we normally breathe?

options.A: It relies entirely on cellular metabolism
options.B: It uses the diaphragm instead of external machinery
options.C: It pushes air into the lungs instead of creating negative pressure
options.D: It only removes carbon dioxide without giving oxygen

explanation: Think of normal breathing like pulling air in by expanding your chest (negative pressure). Machines or manual bags do the opposite—they gently push air right in!

question: What is the primary action a nurse should take when stepping away from a computer terminal on the ward?

options.A: Leave the charting page open for quick access
options.B: Unplug the internet router from the wall
options.C: Lock the computer screen
options.D: Turn off the main hospital power

explanation: Locking your workstation prevents unauthorized people from viewing or altering confidential patient records while you are away. [learn more](GNS113_U1_T9#GNS113_U1_T9_h6)

question: Why is classifying viruses different from classifying bacteria?

options.A: Viruses lack cellular structure and need a host cell to replicate
options.B: Viruses possess both DNA and RNA simultaneously in all groups
options.C: Viruses can be easily stained with standard Gram stain reagents
options.D: Viruses are classified entirely by their ability to form spores

explanation: Because viruses aren't even fully living cells on their own, they hijack human host cells to multiply, making them totally unique to study!

question: What is one of the main ways community health nurses use incidence data?

options.A: Managing the stock of non-medical office stationery
options.B: Spotting unusual disease spikes to trigger quick responses
options.C: Determining the structural engineering needs of bridges
options.D: Calculating the personal income tax of local residents

explanation: Exactly! Nurses keep an eye on incidence so they can spot outbreaks early and jump into action to protect the community.

question: Why are generic drugs generally much more affordable than brand name drugs?

options.A: The government subsidizes all generic manufacturing costs in local factories
options.B: Generic medications are manufactured in smaller quantities than brand drugs
options.C: Generic drugs use lower quality active chemicals to reduce production expenses
options.D: Makers of generic drugs do not carry the original research and marketing costs

explanation: Developing a new drug takes billions in research and advertising. Generic makers skip those initial costs, which is why their prices are much friendlier to patients' pockets.

question: Why do human-made disasters often cause deep psychological trauma and feelings of betrayal?

options.A: They never cause physical injuries, leaving survivors confused about danger
options.B: The element of human negligence or malice creates strong feelings of betrayal
options.C: Psychological symptoms disappear faster because the disaster is man-made
options.D: Victims are always blamed publicly for causing the emergency situation

explanation: That makes total sense—knowing an accident could have been prevented by someone else's carelessness leaves survivors feeling angry and deeply betrayed.

question: During a special ultrasound procedure (saline infusion sonohysterography), sterile saline is gently injected into the uterus. Why?

options.A: To distend the cavity and create a sharp contrast for the ultrasound images
options.B: To numb the internal walls of the uterus prior to a biopsy
options.C: To completely dissolve small endometrial polyps without medication
options.D: To wash away any bacterial infections before surgery starts

explanation: You got it! The fluid puffs up the uterine space like blowing up a tiny balloon, making it much easier for the ultrasound to spot polyps or fibroids.

question: Why should digital health training be part of nursing education?

options.A: To prepare students for tech-driven healthcare environments
options.B: To replace clinical hospital practice with computer games
options.C: To ensure nurses never have to speak to patients in person
options.D: To make nursing school programs shorter and easier

explanation: Spot on! Healthcare is evolving with technology, and learning these skills early sets you up for success in the modern field.

question: Why is it important for nurses to understand water microbiology?

options.A: To help trace disease outbreaks and educate communities
options.B: To measure the exact depth of local rivers
options.C: To design large municipal water treatment plants
options.D: To chemically synthesize new antibiotics for hospitals

explanation: Nurses need this knowledge to connect water sources to community illnesses and teach safe hygiene habits. [learn more](GST114_U3_T3#GST114_U3_T3_h1)

question: Which ethical rule guides how resources are shared when supplies are very scarce during a disaster?

options.A: Giving the newest supplies only to wealthy donors
options.B: Treating every person strictly on a first-come, first-served basis
options.C: Justice and doing the greatest good for the greatest number
options.D: Refusing care until formal legal contracts are signed

explanation: You've got it! In mass disasters, we shift from treating just one person to figuring out how to do the greatest good for the whole community fairly.

question: If a patient just had surgery, which food category is most important to help close up that incision?

options.A: Energy-giving foods
options.B: Protective foods
options.C: Body-building foods
options.D: Perishable foods

explanation: You nailed it! Body-building foods are rich in proteins, which act like bricks and mortar to fix cut tissues and heal wounds.

question: Why would a patient with severe facial swelling get a tracheostomy instead of a normal breathing tube through the mouth?

options.A: It lets the patient speak normally right away
options.B: It bypasses the blocked upper airway completely
options.C: It stops all future lung infections completely
options.D: It needs zero nursing checks afterward

explanation: When facial trauma blocks the upper airway, a tracheostomy makes a fresh, clear pathway below the blockage. You're doing great!

question: What is a 'steroid flare' that some patients experience after a joint injection?

options.A: An immediate permanent cure of all joint stiffness
options.B: A sudden rash spread all over the patient's face
options.C: A temporary increase in joint pain before the medication starts working
options.D: A permanent allergic reaction requiring emergency surgery

explanation: Some patients feel extra soreness for a day or two when steroid crystals irritate the joint before calming down. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T9#GNS125_U3_T9_h7)

question: In a healthcare setting, what does 'resource allocation' mean?

options.A: Calculating the exact profit made by a pharmacy
options.B: The process of admitting patients to private rooms
options.C: Writing new nursing textbooks for students
options.D: How funds, staff, and supplies are distributed

explanation: Great! Resource allocation is simply deciding how to share out available money, materials, and staff to where they are needed most.

question: Which type of sensory receptor specifically picks up physical changes like pressure and vibration?

options.A: Thermoreceptors
options.B: Photoreceptors
options.C: Mechanoreceptors
options.D: Chemoreceptors

explanation: Think of 'mechano' as movement! Mechanoreceptors are the clever nerve endings that convert physical touch and pressure into signals your brain understands.

question: What is the core idea behind deductive reasoning?

options.A: Trusting a senior doctor purely because of their title
options.B: Moving from a general premise down to a specific conclusion
options.C: Accepting traditional habits without asking any questions
options.D: Gathering random facts until a pattern appears by chance

explanation: Deduction takes a known general rule and applies it to a specific situation to figure out what follows.

question: Which action best reflects a comprehensive psychiatric nursing assessment?

options.A: Reviewing the patient's financial records to determine their income
options.B: Exploring the patient's biological, psychological, and social history
options.C: Asking only about the exact moment the patient started feeling sad
options.D: Focusing solely on laboratory blood test results and vital signs

explanation: A thorough nursing assessment investigates all areas of the biopsychosocial model to understand the full picture of the patient's condition. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T4#GNS314_U2_T4_h8)

question: At what point in the hospital workflow should waste segregation take place?

options.A: Inside the municipal waste truck during transit to the dump site
options.B: At the final incineration plant before burning begins
options.C: At the exact point of origin where the waste is generated
options.D: By the sanitary inspectors during their weekly hospital visits

explanation: Spot on! Sorting must happen immediately at the bedside or treatment area so hazardous and general waste never mix. Brilliant!

question: How do vaccines work to protect a child's body against infections?

options.A: By stimulating the immune system to produce antibodies
options.B: By coating the stomach lining to block germ absorption
options.C: By increasing the body temperature to kill viruses
options.D: By providing immediate chemical destruction of all bacteria

explanation: Exactly! Vaccines introduce safe, weakened parts of a germ to train the immune system so it knows how to fight back if the real disease ever shows up.

question: Why must observations be independent when doing a Chi-Square test?

options.A: To eliminate the need for calculating expected frequencies
options.B: To guarantee that all data points are continuous numbers
options.C: To ensure the sample size is always larger than one thousand
options.D: To prevent the same patient from being counted in multiple cells

explanation: Exactly! Independent observations mean each patient is only counted once, keeping our groups separate and our results accurate.

question: A nurse finishes emptying a utility bin filled with used dressings and removes her heavy utility gloves. What is the immediate next step she should take?

options.A: Drink clean water to prevent dehydration
options.B: Perform hand hygiene with soap and water or alcohol rub
options.C: Write an incident report in the ward register
options.D: Put on a fresh pair of sterile surgical gloves

explanation: Hand hygiene is always mandatory immediately after taking off gloves, as microscopic tears in gloves can let germs reach the skin. [learn more](GST114_U6_T12#GST114_U6_T12_h8)

question: Why is it important to involve traditional leaders and local birth attendants in primary health care?

options.A: They hold significant influence over community beliefs and healthcare-seeking behaviors
options.B: They are responsible for funding all primary health care clinics
options.C: They possess advanced medical degrees recognized by the nursing council
options.D: They act as legal inspectors of government health budgets

explanation: Brilliant! When respected local leaders are on board, community members are much more likely to trust nurses and use clinic services.

question: What does an Incremental Cost-Effectiveness Ratio (ICER) tell a nurse administrator?

options.A: The exact percentage of patients who will refuse medication
options.B: The total yearly budget needed to run the emergency department
options.C: The extra cost required to gain one additional unit of health outcome
options.D: The net profit generated by surgical procedures over a quarter

explanation: ICER simply asks: 'Is paying extra for this new treatment worth the extra health benefit we get?' It measures that trade-off.

question: A patient with a mild fever and routine vaccination needs visits a nearby facility staffed by community health workers. Which level of care is this?

options.A: Quaternary level of care
options.B: Tertiary level of care
options.C: Secondary level of care
options.D: Primary level of care

explanation: Spot on! Community clinics handling everyday things like immunizations and mild fevers are right at the primary care level.

question: You feel a new mother's uterus and notice it feels soft, boggy, and pushed to the right. What should you do right away?

options.A: Prepare the patient for immediate surgery
options.B: Administer a dose of oral iron tablets
options.C: Encourage the mother to empty her bladder
options.D: Apply a warm compress to the lower back

explanation: Wonderful clinical thinking! A full bladder often pushes the womb out of place and stops it from tightening up. Once she pees, the womb usually firms right back up!

question: How does a vasectomy change a man's semen volume after surgery?

options.A: It becomes completely clear and watery
options.B: It stays almost exactly the same
options.C: It drops to zero immediately
options.D: It increases to make up for lost sperm

explanation: Spot on! Sperm only make up a tiny fraction of semen, so blocking their path doesn't noticeably change the amount of fluid.

question: When does the second stage of labor end?

options.A: At the onset of true contractions
options.B: When the cervix is fully dilated
options.C: At the birth of the baby
options.D: When the placenta is delivered

explanation: The second stage spans from full cervical dilation all the way until the infant is completely delivered. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T50#GNS214_U1_T50_h3)

question: What do we mean by cross-contamination in the kitchen?

options.A: The transfer of harmful germs from raw food to ready-to-eat food
options.B: Mixing different brands of cooking oil together in a pot
options.C: Cooking food at a temperature that is far too high
options.D: Storing dry goods in the same room as cleaning chemicals

explanation: Cross-contamination happens when germs move from raw items (like meat) onto foods that won't be cooked any further. Keep up the great work!

question: Besides relieving pressure, what is another major reason for doing a paracentesis?

options.A: To check the patient's blood glucose level
options.B: To test the fluid for infection
options.C: To assess how well the kidneys filter urea
options.D: To measure the exact size of the liver

explanation: Taking a small sample of the fluid helps the lab check if there's any hidden infection lurking in the abdomen.

question: Why is the needle directed just over the top of the lower rib during insertion?
